'''Sara E. Skrabalak''' is a James H. Rudy Professor at [[Indiana University Bloomington|Indiana University]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.chem.indiana.edu/faculty/sara-e-skrabalak/|title=Sara E. Skrabalak :Department of Chemistry|website=www.chem.indiana.edu|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref> Skrabalak leads a research group in the department of chemistry which focuses on the development of new [[nanomaterials]]. She has an adjunct appointment in the department of intelligent systems engineering.

== Early life and education ==
Skrabalak was born on March 12, 1980, in [[Altoona, Pennsylvania]], and grew up in [[Indiana, Pennsylvania]].<ref name="thesis-skrabalak-2007" />

Skrabalak obtained her B.S. from [[Washington University in St. Louis]] (chemistry, 2002)]. She conducted research with [[William Buhro]] while there, focused on nanotube synthesis by chemical vapor deposition methods. She received the Sowden Award from Washington University in St. Louis for her undergraduate research. She graduated [[summa cum laude]] and was inducted into [[Phi Beta Kappa]] and [[Sigma Xi]].

She received her Ph.D. in chemistry at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign|University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]] in the laboratory of [[Kenneth S. Suslick|Kenneth Suslick]] (2006). Her thesis research focused on the aerosol synthesis of porous materials, and she was the recipient of the T.S. Piper Thesis Research Award from the chemistry department.<ref name="thesis-skrabalak-2007">{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/304856355/ |title=Porous materials prepared by ultrasonic spray pyrolysis |date=2007 |publisher=[[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]] |degree=Ph.D. |last=Skrabalak |first=Sara |id={{ProQuest|304856355}}|url-access=subscription |oclc=351551655}}</ref> Her postdoctoral research was conducted at the [[University of Washington]] with [[Xingde Li]] and [[Younan Xia]]. There she was introduced to colloidal metal nanoparticle synthesis and their biomedical applications.

==Career==
Skrabalak joined the faculty in the department of chemistry at Indiana University in 2008 and advanced to the rank of full professor in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.indiana.edu/~skrablab/docs/Skrabalak_CV.pdf|title=Indiana University Bloomington|last=|first=|date=|website=|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref> The Provost named Skrabalak a Rudy Professor in 2015. Skrabalak served as the 2016 Nanoscience Chair for the Division of Inorganic Chemistry for the [[American Chemical Society]]. She has been an associate editor for the journal [[Nanoscale (journal)|''Nanoscale'']] ([[Royal Society of Chemistry]]) before being appointed editor-in-chief of the journal ''[[Chemistry of Materials]]'' and ''ACS Materials Letters''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sara E. Skrabalak appointed as editor-in-chief of Chemistry of Materials and ACS Materials Letters |url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/pressroom/newsreleases/2020/november/sara-e-skrabalak-appointed-as-editor-in-chief-of-chemistry-of-materials-and-acs-materials-letters.html |website=acs.org |access-date=15 December 2020 |date=9 November 2020}}</ref>

In addition to her group's research innovations, her research team volunteers at [[WonderLab|Wonderlab]], a Museum of Science, Health, & Technology in Bloomington, IN. She also encourages undergraduate students at Indiana University to return to their local high schools to discuss their experiences as science majors through the Science Ambassadors Program.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.indiana.edu/~skrablab/outreach.shtml|title=Skrabalak Research Group: Department of Chemistry: Indiana University Bloomington|website=www.indiana.edu|access-date=2019-03-10}}</ref>

Skrabalak's team is affiliated with the [[Indiana Innovation Institute]] (IN3), a research institute which seeks to address problems of particular interest and relevance to the [[United States Department of Defense|U.S. Department of Defense]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.iu.edu/stories/2019/01/iub/07-sara-skrabalak-in3-indiana-innovation-institute.html|title=High-tech security could be 100,000 times thinner than a human hair|last=Martin|first=Steve|date=2019-01-07|website=News at IU|language=en|access-date=2019-03-11}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.iu.edu/stories/2019/01/iub/18-david-crandall-in3-indiana-innovation-institute.html|title=Ensuring the integrity of integrated circuits|last=Martin|first=Steve|date=2019-01-18|website=News at IU|language=en|access-date=2019-03-11}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.iu.edu/stories/2019/02/iu/04-indiana-innovation-institute-in3-advances-high-tech-researchers-work.html|title=Indiana University collaborates with Indiana Innovation Institute|last=Martin|first=Steve|date=2019-02-04|website=News at IU|language=en|access-date=2019-03-11}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.purdue.edu/newsroom/releases/2018/Q3/ultra-secure,-ultra-reliable-trusted-microelectronics-development-project-will-focus-on-hardware-first.html|title=Ultra-secure, ultra-reliable trusted microelectronics development project will focus on hardware first|last=Service|first=Purdue News|website=www.purdue.edu|language=en|access-date=2019-03-11}}</ref>

== Research and notable publications ==
Skrabalak's work centers on the synthesis of new nanomaterials and elucidation of structure-property correlations. Her team has worked across diverse classes of nanomaterials, including metallic nanostructures and advanced transformations thereof as well as metal oxides, sulfides, and nitrides. Skralabak is particularly well-known for application and development of novel synthetic methods to advance nanomaterials with control of crystal shape. These methods include ultrasound spray strategies. The synthesized nanomaterials are applied to applications in catalysis, photocatalysis, separations, chemical sensing, and secured electronics.
